Conversely, $\langle x \rangle M = M\langle x \rangle = G$ holds iff $|\langle x \rangle M| = |G|$, i.e., $[\langle x \rangle : \langle x \rangle \cap M] = [G : M]$.

**Counterexample: $G = A_4$, $M = \langle (123) \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}_3$.**

**$P_G(M) = G$.** The Klein four-group $V_4$ is normal in $A_4$, so $V_4$ permutes with every subgroup, in particular with $M$. Since $V_4 \cap M = \{e\}$ and $|V_4|\cdot|M| = 4\cdot 3 = 12 = |G|$, we get $V_4 M = G$. Thus $P_G(M) \geq \langle V_4, M\rangle = G$, so $P_G(M) = G$.

In every case, $[\langle x\rangle : \langle x\rangle \cap M] \in \{2, 3\}$, never $4 = [G:M]$. Therefore $|\langle x\rangle M| \in \{6, 9\} \neq 12 = |G|$ for all $x \in G\setminus M$, so $\langle x\rangle M \neq G$.

$$\langle x\rangle M = \{e, (123), (132), (12)(34), (243), (143)\},$$
$$M\langle x\rangle = \{e, (123), (132), (12)(34), (134), (234)\}.$$
These sets differ (e.g., $(243) \in \langle x\rangle M \setminus M\langle x\rangle$), confirming $\langle x\rangle M \neq M\langle x\rangle$.

In $A_4$, the permutizer condition is satisfied via the normal subgroup $V_4$ permuting with $M$, yet no individual element outside $M$ generates a cyclic subgroup that permutes with $M$ to give all of $G$.
